title: The Press Expedition, 1889-90
status: complete_first_pass; verified_2026_10_08 (VERIFY.md): every quote re-fetched and found verbatim; seven secondary lines from copyrighted modern articles or Wikipedia removed
summary: Six men (five finished), four dogs and two mules, sent by the Seattle Press, crossed the Olympic Mountains north to south in the hard winter and spring of 1889-90: up the Elwha from Port Angeles (Dec 1889 - Apr 1890), over Low Divide (early May 1890) and down the North Fork Quinault to Lake Quinault and the Pacific (May 20, 1890). It was the first documented crossing of the range. Their route is close to our classic trip elwha_to_north_fork_quinault.
credit_line_for_game: Facts about the Press Expedition draw in part on Robert L. Wood, Across the Olympic Mountains: The Press Expedition, 1889-90 (The Mountaineers and University of Washington Press, 1967). No text by Wood is reproduced. Quotations are from public-domain newspapers of 1889-90 and The Mountaineer (1907).
copyright_rules_applied: No sentence from any Robert L. Wood book appears in this file. Facts that trace to Wood are restated in our own words and tagged WOOD1967.
quote_pool holds only text from U.S. publications of 1889-1907 (public domain: published in the U.S. before 1931), each read against a page image (or flagged where only partly checked).
secondary_quote_pool holds 1889-90 words (public domain) that we saw only as transcribed by modern writers; verify each against the 1890 Press before shipping.
Modern articles (Peninsula Daily News, Seattle Times, Wikipedia) are used for facts only, paraphrased.

primary_text_status.seattle_press_1890_07_16: Not found online. The Seattle Press (1886-1891) does not appear to be digitized in Chronicling America, and the Washington Digital Newspapers site refused automated access. Known copies: a photostat and clipped sections in the Robert L. Wood papers and the Meany file at UW Special Collections (UW_WOOD_FA); the Seattle Public Library listed the Seattle Press among its Central Library holdings in 2010 (unverified). Carsten Lien's Exploring the Olympic Mountains (Mountaineers Books, 2001) reprints the report, but as a modern edition it was not used.
public_domain_substitutes_used: MTN1907 (condensed 'as far as possible ... just as published')
SDRU1890 (summary plus Barnes's Jan. 14 journal entry and the full name list)
Other 1889-90 newspapers on Chronicling America (WS1889, MCJ1890a, WS1890, ES1890, SPI1890a, FH1890, SPI1890b)
primary_text_status.next_step: Ask UW Special Collections (speccoll@uw.edu) for a scan of the July 16, 1890 Press to verify the secondary quotes and add diary lines about the bears, the dogs and Low Divide.

members.name: James Halbold Christie
members.spelling_note: NPS HRS spells the middle name Helbold; Wikipedia uses Halbold.
members.background: Served with Canadian military forces and had spent about three years on an Arctic expedition. Wrote to the Press from North Yakima in November 1889 asking to lead the party.
members.after: By mid-June 1890 he had signed on as foreman of Israel C. Russell's National Geographic Society expedition to Mount St. Elias, Alaska, taking two bear dogs from the Olympic trip (ES1890).

members.name: Charles Adams Barnes
members.background: Former military/Revenue Service officer who had been in business in California. Kept the main journal, drew the map (NPS calls it the first published map of Lake Crescent, and the first to show the major peaks and valleys of the eastern interior) and took the photographs.
members.after: His brother Pierre Barnes took up a claim near Lake Crescent in 1890 (Seattle P-I, May 22, 1890, p.9).
members.named_for_him: Mount Barnes (the name has since moved to a different peak; see place_names)

members.name: John Henry Crumback
members.background: Prospector, cowboy and hunter in the Northwest Territories before Seattle. Nearly fainted in the icy Elwha on January 14, 1890 (Barnes's journal). Staked a squatter's claim by the Elwha on March 21, 1890.
members.named_for_him: Crumback River (their name for the East Fork Quinault; not in use)

members.name: John William Sims
members.background: Six years in the British army, then hunting, trapping, prospecting and trading.

members.name: Christopher O'Connell Hayes
members.named_for_him: Hayes River (still in use; node hayes_river)

members.name: Dr. Harris Boyle Runnalls
members.spelling_note: NPS HRS: Harris Boyle Runnalls (sometimes Runnals); Peninsula Daily News 2009: Horace B. Runnals. Unresolved.
members.role: Physician and naturalist ("the doctor" in Barnes's journal)
members.background: Left the party on February 3, 1890 (PDN says for a family emergency), so only five crossed the range.

dogs.name: Daisy
dogs.fate: Not recorded in the sources read for this file.

dogs.name: Tweed
dogs.fate: One of the two bear dogs. Probably one of the 'two famous dogs' Christie took to Alaska in June 1890 (inference: the Evening Star does not name them).

dogs.name: Bud
dogs.fate: One of the two bear dogs. Probably the other dog that went to Alaska with Christie (same inference).

dogs.name: Dike
dogs.fate: Killed by a bull elk (kicked in the head) in Press Valley, spring 1890.

animals.dogs_notes: Four dogs started. The survivors slept with the men in the snow, hunted, ate the last of the bacon, and ran down the bears near Low Divide that kept the men from starving. Christie's two bear dogs were described in 1890 as crosses of a Russian bear dog and a Scotch collie (ES1890).

mules.name: Jennie
mules.fate: Fell off the steep ridge the party called the Devil's Backbone, above today's old Elwha Ranger Station, and died. Her load of about 200 lb included the 50 lb of colored fire (fireworks) meant to be lit on a peak where Seattle could see it.

mules.name: Dollie
mules.fate: Worn out (living on Oregon grape), she lay down on the wrong-way detour up the Goldie River in April 1890 and would not rise. The men took off her halter and turned her loose. In August 1890 a Sacramento paper joked that a mule was loose 'in the neighborhood of Mount Olympus' for anyone who could catch her.

outfit.weight: About 1,500 lb of supplies when the party left Seattle (SDRU1890, NPS_EXPL); PDN2023a says about 2,000 lb were loaded into the boat on Dec 30, 1889.
outfit.items_1890_list: Flour, bacon, beans, coffee, Winchester rifles, powder and shot, a tent, blankets, fishing tackle, axes, a whipsaw for logs, carpenter tools, mineral-prospecting tools, rope, snowshoes, cooking gear, surveying instruments, and a camera with film for 250 exposures (SDRU1890).
outfit.colored_fire: Fifty pounds of colored fire (signal fireworks), meant to light up a peak that Seattle could see (SDRU1890). Lost with the mule Jennie (ST1997).
outfit.boat_gertie: A flat-bottomed boat about 30 by 5 ft, built of green lumber and named Gertie. Launched Dec 30 or 31, 1889 and leaked at once. Hauled up the Elwha by towline, the men often waist-deep in icy water, and abandoned about Jan 23, 1890 after gaining only a few miles (sources say 4 to 6) in 10 to 12 days (NPS_EXPL, MTN1907, PDN2009b, PDN2023a, ST1997).

route_on_our_map.where_the_1890_route_left_ours: The party went up the Goldie River (no trail, no node) from near remanns_cabin and came back to the Elwha near camp_wilder. They travelled the lower Elwha by boat and on the valley floor long before today's road and trail; Indian Creek, McDonald's clearing, Griff Creek, the Devil's Backbone, the Quinault forks and Taholah have no nodes. The NPS notes the modern trail follows roughly the Press route except where the party went up the Goldie.

timeline.event: The Seattle Press prints an interview with Gov. Elisha P. Ferry calling the interior an unknown land and daring 'hardy citizens' to explore it.
The Press receives James Christie's letter from North Yakima offering to lead a party into the Olympics that winter.
The six men are photographed in Seattle before leaving.
The party leaves Seattle by steamer (the Evangel) for Port Angeles. A Sacramento paper later said Dec 7; the Port Angeles Commonwealth said they arrived on a Monday (Dec 9).
timeline.node_note: Port Angeles waterfront; the WIC node is the nearest town node.

timeline.event: They leave the end of the county road out of Port Angeles for the Elwha (Seattle Times date). Snow fell on their first night in camp and stopped at about four feet (SDRU1890).
timeline.node_note: Between town and the lower Elwha; no node at the 1889 road end.

timeline.event: Christmas snow; supplies are moved by sled toward the river.
timeline.node_note: Lower Elwha settlements, north of the Madison Falls gate.

timeline.event: The boat Gertie is launched loaded with supplies and leaks at once; the men spend days caulking her.
Gertie is finally watertight and the haul up the Elwha begins.
Barnes's journal: barely a quarter mile gained, two sets of rapids, a log cut out, everyone in the icy river to the belt at 16 degrees F, Crumback close to fainting.
timeline.node_note: Lower Elwha below today's Madison Falls gate (no node).

timeline.event: A log jam at the mouth of Indian Creek stops the boat; local men help drag her over.
timeline.node_note: Indian Creek enters the Elwha north of the Madison Falls gate, near today's US 101 bridge (no node).

timeline.event: Head of navigation: stores are moved ashore and Gertie is abandoned, after 10-12 days and only a few miles. From here the men relay packs and use the mules.
timeline.node_note: Around McDonald's clearing on the lower Elwha (no node).

timeline.event: A Port Townsend paper reports the party back at Port Angeles 'last evening' with two feet of snow within ten miles of town (probably a supply trip; the report credits Barnes as the man in charge).
Snowbound for about two weeks in an empty settler's cabin, then relaying about forty 50-lb packs by snowshoe and sled. Moving 800 lb a mile and a half could take a whole day.
Dr. Runnalls leaves the expedition. Five men go on.
On the Devil's Backbone, a steep ridge above today's old Elwha Ranger Station, the mule Jennie falls to her death with the fireworks.
timeline.node_note: MTN1907 calls the Devil's Backbone the western spur of 'Mt. Eldridge'.

timeline.event: They spend a night in an abandoned Klallam house near the site of the later Glines Canyon dam, and meet a Klallam elk-hunting camp near today's park boundary.
timeline.node_note: Secondary source only; see indigenous_notes before using.

timeline.event: The party reaches the area of Griff Creek on the Elwha.
timeline.node_note: Griff Creek joins the Elwha near the old ranger station (no node).

timeline.event: South end of what later became Lake Mills: beyond here nobody in the settlements could tell them anything. Half the supplies are already gone.
timeline.node_note: The old lakebed below Whiskey Bend; no node at the former south shore.

timeline.event: A member kills a bobcat where a creek meets the Elwha; they call it Wildcat Creek (today's Cat Creek).
timeline.node_note: GNIS places a Cat Creek mouth at 47.971 N, 123.594 W, on the west side just downstream of Whiskey Bend.

timeline.event: Goblin Gates: the whole Elwha pours through a slot of rock about 12 ft wide. Barnes sees faces in the rock and names it. Christie catches fourteen trout in half an hour nearby; deer show no fear.
Geyser Valley: they hear booming bursts that speed up and stop, every few days, and decide they must be geysers. They build a smokehouse and live on elk, deer and steelhead. Everyone has dysentery.
timeline.game_use: The noise was most likely ruffed grouse drumming (PDN2009b). A good mystery for a camp night in Geyser Valley.

timeline.event: Crumback stakes a squatter's claim by the river.
timeline.node_note: Exact spot not stated in the sources read.

timeline.event: Barnes finds very old blazes healed into tree trunks (one with about 210 growth rings over the cut) and old 'wringing posts' used to dress hides, between Geyser Valley and the Lillian River.
timeline.game_use: Evidence that people knew these valleys long before 1890. See indigenous_notes.

timeline.event: They reach the Lillian River, which they name.

Up the Elwha past a great landslide and the 'Semple Plateau', a flat bench on the west side that Barnes takes for an old village site, into the wide upper valley they call Press Valley. Waist-deep snow at camp. In April, gunshots near the main camp set off a scare about strangers.
timeline.node_note: GNIS puts Semple Plateau at 47.843 N, 123.474 W, on the west side between remanns_cabin and hayes_river.

timeline.event: The dog Dike is killed by a bull elk in Press Valley.
A scouting party sees a gap leading away from the Elwha. The party turns up the Goldie River: the wrong way, into steep, trackless side country. Around now the exhausted mule Dollie is turned loose.
timeline.node_note: Goldie River mouth at 47.840 N, 123.470 W (GNIS), next to remanns_cabin; the Goldie itself has no trail or node.

timeline.event: Climbing out of the Goldie with 75-lb packs through snow said to be up to 15 ft deep. From the high ground Christie and Barnes see over the divide ahead, and from then on each man carries a single pack; the relaying is over.
timeline.node_note: Upper Goldie and the ridges north of Mount Wilder (no trail or node).

timeline.event: They name the Bailey Range, after the Press's owner William E. Bailey.
timeline.node_note: Seen from the Goldie/Elwha divide; the range is visible from hurricane_ridge_visitor_center.

timeline.event: Christie and Barnes name Mount Seattle for the city.
timeline.node_note: Mount Seattle rises west of Low Divide.

timeline.event: Camp in the upper Goldie drainage below Mount Wilder; then they drop back to the upper Elwha valley floor (about four hours down).
Up the last of the Elwha, past the place later called Chicago Camp, toward the gap between Mount Seattle and Mount Christie.
timeline.node_note: No evidence in these sources that the party entered elwha_basin itself; the basin is the view to the west.

timeline.event: They name Lake Mary and Lake Margaret and find the pass, which they call Elwha Pass (today's Low Divide, 3,602 ft in our data). Beside a big boulder, water seen through an opening in the snow is flowing south: they are over the top.
Just past the divide, with almost nothing left but flour soup, the dogs bring three bears to bay. The meat (and the men drinking bear grease straight from the pan) saves them from starving.
Snow gives way to rain and dark rain forest on the North Fork Quinault. They pass the Rustler Creek confluence in mid-May.
timeline.node_note: Rustler Creek's exact position relative to our nodes was not verified.

timeline.event: At the junction of the North Fork and the main Quinault they find an empty trapper's cabin, the first sign of other people in about 80 days. That night they eat the last of the flour.
timeline.node_note: The forks are below the North Fork trailhead (no node).

timeline.event: Their raft is swept under a driftwood jam. They lose guns, ammunition, bear skins, fishing tackle and most rock samples. Barnes gets one pack out of the water, and it holds what matters most: the journals, about 250 negatives and the map.
timeline.node_note: Main Quinault between the forks and Lake Quinault (no node).

timeline.event: Settler Frederick S. Antrim of Aberdeen and two Quinault men in a canoe find them; Antrim later canoes them to his cabin near Lake Quinault and feeds them.
timeline.node_note: Upper end of Lake Quinault, where homesteading began in 1889 (see kestner_homestead).

timeline.event: They reach Lake Quinault.
By canoe down the lake and river to the Quinault Indian Agency at the river mouth (Taholah), on the Pacific.
timeline.node_note: Taholah is outside the park and not in our region data.

timeline.event: Five ragged men sail into Aberdeen at 2 a.m.; telegrams from the Press are waiting. Photographed in their rags.
Back in Seattle, 166 days after leaving.
The Evening Star reports Christie hired as foreman of the National Geographic Society's Mount St. Elias expedition, taking two famous bear dogs.
The Seattle Press publishes the report (Wednesday evening): a 24-page edition, with the story on 10 to 16 pages, many engravings from Barnes's photographs, and his map.
The rival Post-Intelligencer reprints a later party's complaint that the Press blazes give out and that no geysers could be heard.

memorable_events.title: The governor's dare
memorable_events.summary: Gov. Ferry called the Olympic interior Washington's great unknown and the Seattle Press dared its readers to explore it. Christie wrote in from North Yakima offering to lead a party, the Press paid for it, and six men left Seattle in December - in winter, so they could be deep in the range by spring.

memorable_events.title: Fifty pounds of fireworks
memorable_events.summary: The outfit included 50 lb of colored fire to set off on a peak where Seattle could see it. It was on the mule Jennie when she fell off the Devil's Backbone.

memorable_events.title: The boat Gertie
memorable_events.summary: A leaky 30-ft flat-bottomed boat hauled up the winter Elwha by men standing in icy water. On Jan. 14 they gained a quarter mile. After about ten days and only a few miles she was left on the bank.

memorable_events.title: Relays in the snow
memorable_events.summary: Snowbound for two weeks, then moving camp in 50-lb packs, each man walking the same stretch eight times. Some days a mile and a half was all they could move.

memorable_events.title: Jennie falls
memorable_events.summary: On the steep Devil's Backbone ridge the mule Jennie slipped and fell to her death. Everything she carried went onto the men's backs.

memorable_events.title: The Goblin Gates
memorable_events.summary: Barnes saw faces in the rock where the Elwha squeezes through a 12-ft slot and named it. Robert L. Wood later wrote an article titled 'The Goblin Gates Refound'.

memorable_events.title: The geysers that weren't
memorable_events.summary: In the valley they named Geyser Valley the men heard bursts that started slow, sped up and stopped, and blamed hidden geysers. Nobody ever found one. The sound fits a drumming ruffed grouse.

memorable_events.title: Older blazes than theirs
memorable_events.summary: Cutting their own three-blaze trail, the party found far older cuts healed over in living trees, and posts for working hides: signs that people had travelled these valleys long before 1890.

memorable_events.title: Sick and half-fed
memorable_events.summary: By the end of February half the food was gone and every man had dysentery. They smoked elk, deer and steelhead in Geyser Valley to stretch the flour.

memorable_events.title: Dike and the elk
memorable_events.summary: In Press Valley a bull elk kicked the dog Dike in the head and killed him.

memorable_events.title: The wrong way up the Goldie
memorable_events.summary: Thinking a side valley was the way to the Quinault, they spent days in steep, trackless side country, climbing out through deep snow with heavy packs. Dollie the mule lay down there and was set free. Their own trail notes later told others to keep to Press Valley instead.

memorable_events.title: Naming the range
memorable_events.summary: From the high ground they named the Bailey Range, Mount Seattle, Mount Christie and dozens more, mostly after newspapermen. Lake Mary and Lake Margaret and 'Elwha Pass' came last.

memorable_events.title: Three bears at the divide
memorable_events.summary: Down to flour soup after the dogs got into the bacon, the men were saved when the dogs brought three bears to bay just past the divide. They drank the grease straight from the pan.
memorable_events.caution: Modern parallel for the game: food storage and bear canisters (park rules), never hunting.

memorable_events.title: The raft and the records
memorable_events.summary: On the main Quinault their raft went under a driftwood jam. Guns, ammunition, skins and specimens were lost; Barnes got one pack out of the water, and it held the journals, the negatives and the map.

memorable_events.title: Antrim's cabin
memorable_events.summary: The settler Frederick S. Antrim, travelling with two Quinault men by canoe, found them and fed them at his cabin near Lake Quinault. The party later named an 'Antrim Range' for him.

memorable_events.title: Aberdeen, 2 a.m.
memorable_events.summary: Five ragged men reached Aberdeen in the small hours, found telegrams from the Press, and wired for money to get home.

memorable_events.title: The July 16 report
memorable_events.summary: The Press printed a 24-page edition with the story, engravings made from Barnes's photographs and his map. Other papers praised it; the rival P-I predicted the names would not last and later printed a critic who could not find the blazes or hear the geysers.

memorable_events.title: Epilogue: to Alaska
memorable_events.summary: A month after the crossing Christie signed on for the National Geographic Society's Mount St. Elias expedition and took two of the bear dogs with him.

place_names_summary.how_many: MTN1907 says about fifty names were given. The SDRU1890 list prints 47 entries (including the Elwha, which it explains as 'an Indian name signifying elk' - an 1890 claim the game should not repeat as fact without the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe). NPS (1983) counted at least eighteen still in use.
place_names_summary.pattern: Mostly the party's own members and the country's newspaper owners and editors, chosen to win the national press's attention. The rival Seattle P-I predicted on July 17, 1890 that the names would not last (see quote q45-q46); about half did not.
place_names_summary.verify_before_use: Name shifts (Barnes/Wilder/Childs, Ferry/Pulitzer, Lawson/Grady) come from Wikipedia, which traces them to Wood and to Parratt's Gods & Goblins (1984). Check them in Wood before printing them.

indigenous_notes.note: The Press route starts in the homeland of the Klallam (S'Klallam) people on the lower Elwha, today the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe, a sovereign, federally recognized nation that has lived there since time immemorial and signed the 1855 Treaty of Point No Point. It ends in Quinault country: Lake Quinault, the lower Quinault River and the Quinault Indian Agency at Taholah, today the Quinault Indian Nation.

The 1889-90 Press framed the interior as never trodden by anyone, 'white or Indian'. NPS says Native Americans had long known the interior. The party's own report contradicts the myth: very old blazes healed into trees (one with about 210 rings over the cut), old hide-working posts, old trails, and a bench Barnes took for a long-abandoned village site (MTN1907). The game should not repeat 'first to see' or 'unexplored' claims except as quoted 1890 attitudes, clearly framed.

A modern columnist reports a Klallam elk-hunting camp near today's park boundary (Christie dismissed the hunters as knowing nothing of the country) and a night in an abandoned Klallam house near the later Glines Canyon dam site. At the end, two Quinault men in a canoe were with the settler Antrim when he found the starving party, and Quinault country carried them by canoe to the coast. Do not invent names, speech or scenes for these people.

The 1890 list explains 'Elwha' as an Indian name meaning elk. Do not present that, or the origin of 'Queets' or 'Quinault', as settled fact in game text without checking with the tribes. The Klallam and Quinault have their own names for these places; the game should ask before using any of them.

indigenous_notes.topic: The Elwha dams and the river today
indigenous_notes.note: The Elwha and Glines Canyon dams (built in the early 1900s) blocked salmon and flooded Klallam homelands and cultural sites; their removal began September 17, 2011 and finished in 2014. Our glines_canyon_overlook node stands on the old dam. Any story beat there should credit the tribe's long campaign and avoid describing cultural sites.

Before using any Indigenous content tied to this route (the Semple Plateau 'village site', the old blazes, the hunting camp, the abandoned house, the canoe rescue, place-name meanings), contact the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe (elwha.org, info@elwha.org, 360-452-8471) and the Quinault Indian Nation (Taholah, 360-276-8211). Do not retell sacred stories. Recorded here as facts only, with no cultural interpretation.
